title: Maximum Employees to Be Invited to a Meeting
statement:
There are `n` employees, numbered `0` to `n - 1`, and employee `i` has one favorite colleague, `favorite[i]`, who is never `i` themself. You are inviting people to a meeting around a single round table with room for any number of guests. An employee will attend only if one of the two seats directly beside them is taken by their favorite colleague (so that colleague has to be invited as well). With exactly two guests, each one sits next to the other.

Return the largest number of employees you can invite and seat so that every guest sits beside their favorite colleague.
notes:
## Intuition

Draw an arrow from each employee to their favorite. Every employee has exactly one outgoing arrow, so each connected group is one cycle with trees of chains flowing into it. Only two kinds of table work:

- **One whole cycle of length 3 or more.** Each guest's two seats are already taken by the cycle neighbours, so nobody else can join. Its value is the cycle length.
- **Mutual pairs (cycles of length 2) with tails.** The pair `a, b` sit together, which frees one side of each. The longest chain of people leading into `a` can sit in a line on `a`'s side, and likewise for `b`. Such lines have open ends, so every mutual pair, with its two longest tails, can be placed side by side at the same table.

The answer is the larger of the longest big cycle and the sum over all mutual pairs. Trying every seating order (the brute force) is exponential; peeling the trees off with a topological sort finds both quantities in linear time.

## Approach

1. Count `indegree`: how many people name each employee as favorite.
2. Run Kahn's algorithm: start a `queue` with everyone nobody favors, and repeatedly remove `person`, pushing their longest tail length one step forward into `depth[next]`. Whatever is never removed lies on a cycle.
3. Walk each remaining cycle once, marking its members with `indegree = 0`, to get its `length`.
4. A cycle of length 2 adds `depth[i] + depth[favorite[i]] + 2` to `pairTotal`; a longer one updates `longestCycle`.
5. Return the larger of `longestCycle` and `pairTotal`.

## Example 1, step by step

`favorite = [2,2,1,2]`: `indegree = [0,1,3,0]`. The queue starts with `0` and `3`; each sets `depth[2] = 1` and lowers `indegree[2]` to 1, so `2` stays. Employees `1` and `2` remain and form a cycle of length 2, giving `pairTotal = depth[1] + depth[2] + 2 = 0 + 1 + 2 = 3`. There is no longer cycle, so the answer is `3`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): each employee enters the queue at most once and each cycle is walked once.
- Space: O(n) for `indegree`, `depth` and `queue`.

## Pitfalls

- Tails help only cycles of length 2; adding them to a longer cycle overcounts.
- Mutual pairs are **summed**, not maximised: all of them fit at one table together.
- Only the longest tail on each side of a pair counts, which is why `depth` keeps a maximum.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `indegree` | how many remaining people favor each employee; 0 once removed or visited |
| `depth` | longest chain of people leading into an employee |
| `queue`, `head` | Kahn's queue of employees not on a cycle, and its read position |
| `person`, `next` | the removed employee and their favorite |
| `length`, `current` | size of the cycle being walked and the walker |
| `longestCycle` | largest cycle of length at least 3 |
| `pairTotal` | combined size of all mutual pairs with their tails |
